title: Ambani's Jio Files for What Could Be India's Biggest IPO Ever — and This Time, No One Is Cashing Out
excerpt: Jio Platforms has filed draft papers with India's markets regulator for a fresh-issue-only listing of up to 27 crore shares, a deal market estimates put near ₹36,000 crore at a valuation of roughly ₹12.5 lakh crore — with the proceeds aimed squarely at paying down debt rather than handing existing investors an exit.
body:
It has been promised, deferred and dissected for years. On Friday, Mukesh Ambani finally set the clock ticking: Jio Platforms, the telecom-and-technology arm of Reliance Industries, filed its draft papers for a stock-market listing that could be the largest in India's history.

## The Deal on Paper

The board of Jio Platforms approved its Draft Red Herring Prospectus — the formal disclosure document that opens an IPO process — on June 19 and lodged it with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the BSE and the NSE the same day. The offering is structured as a fresh issue of up to 27 crore equity shares, each with a face value of ₹10, at a price to be set through book-building.

The numbers, even in draft form, are staggering. Market estimates peg the raise at up to roughly ₹36,000 crore, valuing Jio Platforms at about ₹12.5 lakh crore. Brokerages put the company's worth at somewhere between $130 billion and $180 billion — a range that, at the top end, would make this one of the largest public offerings ever attempted in the country. Reliance has not yet disclosed a final issue size; the public portion is widely speculated to be around $4 billion.

Calling it "a deeply emotional moment," Ambani told shareholders at Reliance's annual general meeting that his children — Akash, Isha and Anant Ambani — are leading the IPO process. The listing, he said, would "demonstrate to the world that India can build technology companies of global scale, global capability and global value."



> **"Calling it "a deeply emotional moment," Ambani told shareholders at Reliance's annual general meeting that his children — Akash, Isha and Anant Ambani — are leading the IPO process."**


## Why "Fresh Issue Only" Matters

The most consequential detail is structural. Earlier plans had cast the IPO as an "offer for sale," in which existing shareholders — including marquee backers Meta, with a 9.99 percent stake, and Google, with 7.73 percent, alongside Gulf sovereign funds and private-equity giants such as KKR and Vista — would sell down part of their holdings and cash out. That has been scrapped.


![Mukesh Ambani — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/69/Mukesh_Ambani.jpg)


Instead, every rupee raised will come from new shares, with none of the early investors heading for the door. "Investors were not keen to sell and wanted to stay invested for the long term," one source involved told Reuters. The signal to the market is pointed: the people who know Jio best want to keep their chips on the table.

The money has a clear destination. According to the prospectus, the bulk of the net proceeds — about ₹27,500 crore — will go to prepay or repay borrowings of Reliance Jio Infocomm, including external commercial loans taken on in 2024, with the remainder reserved for general corporate purposes. This is a deleveraging story as much as a growth story: a listing designed to clean up the balance sheet of a business that already serves more than 500 million subscribers, the world's second-largest telecom operator by users after China Mobile.

## A Tricky Moment to List

The timing is anything but serene. India's equity markets have cooled in recent months, rattled by the West Asia conflict, volatile oil and a record exodus of foreign portfolio money — more than $30 billion pulled from Indian stocks so far in 2026. The benchmark indices have whipsawed, and the IT sector just touched a three-year low. Jio is stepping into that crosswind, and it is not alone: the NSE, India's largest stock exchange, filed its own draft papers a day earlier, setting up a crowded second half of the year for Indian listings.

A draft filing is also only the starting gun. SEBI approval, final pricing and the eventual listing date all lie ahead, and the headline valuation could shift before shares ever trade.

## Why It Matters for NRIs

For the diaspora, this is the listing many have waited the better part of a decade to see. Jio is woven into the daily life of nearly every Indian family with a smartphone — the data plan, the digital payments, the streaming, increasingly the AI services Ambani keeps promising. Owning a piece of it carries an emotional pull that few other Indian stocks can match, a chance to hold equity in the diaspora's most-used digital utility.

But sentiment is not a strategy. The fresh-issue-only design means NRIs would be buying new shares to fund debt repayment and expansion, not stepping in as insiders step out — a structure that can be read as confidence, or as a company raising capital on its own terms. The valuation is rich, the market is jittery, and the final price is unknown. For NRIs weighing whether to participate through permitted routes, the prudent posture is the same as for any blockbuster IPO: separate the pride of ownership from the arithmetic of price, and wait for the numbers the draft does not yet reveal.
image_caption: Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, whose Jio Platforms has filed draft papers for a record IPO
nri_angle: Jio touches nearly every Indian family with a phone, and its listing is the marquee event NRI investors have waited years for — a chance to own a slice of the diaspora's most-used digital utility, even as the fresh-issue-only structure and a cooled, war-rattled market raise real questions about price and timing.
author: Diaspora Desk
